title: Password Strength Methodology
overview: Password strength is measured in bits of entropy. Higher entropy means more possible combinations and longer time to crack. NIST guidelines emphasize length over complexity.

methods.name: Entropy Calculation
methods.description: Entropy measures the randomness/unpredictability of a password in bits.

formula.name: Password Entropy
formula.expression:
Entropy (bits) = log₂(Pool Size ^ Length)
= Length × log₂(Pool Size)

limitations: Dictionary words have much lower effective entropy

expandedContent.history: The concept of password entropy derives from Claude Shannon's 1948 groundbreaking paper 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication,' which introduced information entropy as a measure of uncertainty. Shannon's work at Bell Labs quantified information content in bits, providing the mathematical foundation for modern cryptography. In the 1970s, as computer systems began requiring password authentication, entropy became the standard metric for evaluating password strength. The US Department of Defense's 1985 'Password Management Guideline' (CSC-STD-002-85) was among the first to formally apply entropy calculations to password policy. As computing power increased exponentially following Moore's Law, minimum entropy requirements have continually risen to stay ahead of brute-force cracking capabilities.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: Password entropy is rooted in information theory and measures the number of bits needed to represent all possible passwords of a given format. The formula H = L x log2(R) calculates entropy where L is length and R is the size of the character pool. Each bit of entropy doubles the number of possible combinations, meaning a 40-bit password has 2^40 (approximately one trillion) possibilities. The time to brute-force a password scales linearly with 2^H, where H is entropy in bits. Modern GPUs can test billions of hashes per second, making passwords under 50 bits of entropy vulnerable. However, entropy assumes truly random character selection. Human-chosen passwords exhibit patterns, dictionary words, and predictable substitutions that dramatically reduce effective entropy. Research by Bonneau (2012) showed that user-chosen passwords average only 10-20 bits of effective entropy regardless of complexity requirements, which is far below the theoretical maximum. This gap between theoretical and effective entropy is why security experts increasingly recommend randomly generated passwords managed by dedicated password managers.
examples: Example 1: An 8-character password using lowercase letters only: Pool = 26, Entropy = 8 x log2(26) = 8 x 4.7 = 37.6 bits. This is considered weak by modern standards.
Example 2: A 12-character password using lowercase, uppercase, digits, and symbols: Pool = 94, Entropy = 12 x log2(94) = 12 x 6.55 = 78.6 bits. This is considered strong.
Example 3: A 4-word passphrase from a 7,776-word dictionary (Diceware): Entropy = 4 x log2(7776) = 4 x 12.93 = 51.7 bits. Memorable yet moderately strong.
expandedContent.comparison: Entropy calculation provides a theoretical maximum strength assuming perfect randomness, while real-world password strength depends heavily on how passwords are generated. Entropy is more precise than rule-based strength meters that simply check for character variety. Unlike NIST guidelines which focus on practical policies, entropy gives a mathematical measure. However, entropy alone cannot account for dictionary attacks, pattern recognition, or social engineering. Zxcvbn, a modern password strength estimator developed by Dropbox, combines entropy estimation with pattern matching for more realistic strength assessment.

pros: Provides a precise mathematical measure of theoretical password strength
Universal metric that can compare different password formats objectively
Scales predictably with password length and character pool size
Helps set evidence-based minimum password requirements
cons: Assumes perfectly random character selection which humans rarely achieve
Does not account for dictionary attacks or common password patterns
Theoretical maximum may vastly overestimate real-world password strength
Cannot measure strength of passwords based on personal information
Does not consider that hashing algorithm speed affects cracking time

methods.name: NIST SP 800-63B Guidelines
methods.description: Modern recommendations prioritize length and checking against compromised password lists.

formula.name: NIST Recommendations
formula.expression:
Minimum: 8 characters
Recommended: 15+ characters
Check against breach databases
No complexity requirements needed if long enough

expandedContent.history: NIST Special Publication 800-63B was first issued in 2004 as part of the Digital Identity Guidelines series. The landmark 2017 revision, led by Paul Grassi, dramatically changed password guidance by removing periodic password expiration requirements and complex composition rules. This shift was influenced by research showing that forced complexity led to weaker passwords as users adopted predictable patterns like 'P@ssw0rd!'. Bill Burr, the original 2003 NIST password guidelines author, publicly acknowledged in 2017 that his earlier advice on complexity requirements was misguided. The 2020 update further emphasized checking passwords against breach databases and supporting longer passphrases, reflecting the evolving understanding that length and uniqueness matter far more than character complexity.
expandedContent.scientificBasis: The NIST guidelines are based on extensive research into human password behavior and attack methodologies. Studies by Florencio and Herley (2007) at Microsoft showed that complexity requirements cause users to create predictable patterns. Credential stuffing attacks, which use passwords from data breaches to compromise other accounts, have become the dominant attack vector, making uniqueness more important than complexity. The guidelines recommend checking passwords against compromised password databases like Have I Been Pwned, which contains billions of breached credentials. Research demonstrates that passwords over 15 characters provide sufficient resistance against brute-force attacks even with current GPU technology. The recommendation against mandatory password rotation is supported by findings that users who must change passwords frequently choose weaker passwords and make minimal, predictable modifications to existing ones, such as incrementing a trailing number. Multi-factor authentication is recommended as a complementary measure, providing defense in depth even when passwords are compromised. The guidelines also prohibit truncating passwords, ensuring that every character contributes to security, and require that all Unicode characters be accepted to support global users and longer passphrases.
examples: Example 1: A compliant password policy requires minimum 8 characters, recommends 15+, checks against a breach database of 800 million compromised passwords, and allows all printable characters including spaces.

Example 2: An organization removes its 90-day password rotation requirement after NIST guidance, instead implementing breach detection monitoring and mandatory change only when compromise is suspected.

Example 3: A user creates a 20-character passphrase 'correct horse battery staple' which passes NIST guidelines despite having no uppercase, numbers, or symbols, because its length provides sufficient entropy.
expandedContent.comparison: NIST guidelines differ significantly from traditional password policies still used by many organizations. Traditional policies require uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols with regular rotation, while NIST recommends length over complexity and no mandatory rotation. The PCI-DSS standard still requires password changes every 90 days, creating tension with NIST guidance. OWASP recommendations align more closely with NIST. Unlike pure entropy calculation, NIST takes a holistic approach considering human behavior, attack patterns, and usability alongside mathematical strength.

pros: Based on extensive research into actual password behavior and attack methods
Prioritizes usability alongside security reducing user frustration
Breach database checking catches the most common attack vector
Regularly updated to reflect current threat landscape
cons: Many organizations are slow to adopt updated guidelines
Compliance frameworks may conflict with NIST recommendations
Breach database checking requires ongoing database maintenance
Guidelines may not address all organizational risk profiles
No mandatory rotation can be problematic if breaches go undetected

footnotes: Character pools: lowercase (26), uppercase (26), digits (10), symbols (~32)
Use password manager for unique passwords per site
Passphrases (4+ random words) are strong and memorable
